sources.title: Children with Shy or Slow to Warm Up Temperaments
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (page dated 4 May 2025)
sources.quote: "slow to warm up," meaning they are uneasy or cautious in new situations or with unfamiliar people. ... Give notice about new people, events, and places. ... follow your child's lead and just watch the action for a while. ... gives a shy child some time to engage in side-by-side play ... Put what you think your child is feeling into words. ... Avoid labels. ... Routines are especially important and comforting.
sources.supports: Slow to warm up children are uneasy or cautious in new situations; tips: give notice about new people, events and places, follow the child's lead and let them watch, side-by-side play, name the feeling, avoid labels, keep routines. Quotes are fragments read through a page fetch, joined with ' ... '. The page is about shy or slow to warm up children in general (toddlers and preschoolers).

sources.title: Shyness in Kids
sources.publisher: CHOP (Children's Hospital of Philadelphia) health tip by Katie K. Lockwood, MD, MEd, 10 Jul 2025
sources.quote: For example, if you're headed to a new park or playground, tell your child about it before you get there ... When you get there, follow your child's lead. ... We have to be very careful about labeling kids or allowing others to label our kids as 'shy' or 'stand-offish'.
sources.supports: Tell the child about a new place before arriving, follow the child's lead when there, and be careful about labels such as shy. Fragments read through a page fetch.

sources.title: How to Help Young Children with Social Anxiety
sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (Katherine Martinelli, reviewed 1 Jul 2026)
sources.quote: Scripting, role-playing and previewing are all excellent tools for the socially anxious kid. ... I'll encourage her to take little steps out of her comfort zone, like starting out watching the other kids,
sources.supports: Previewing and role-playing help a child who is nervous in social situations; a parent's example of little steps out of the comfort zone, starting by watching other kids. The page is about social anxiety; we apply the previewing and small steps to cautious children as an analogy, not as a diagnosis.

sources.title: Helping Kids When They Worry
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (reviewed Oct 2021 by Holly M. Antal, PhD)
sources.quote: When possible, help kids break a new thing into small steps. ... Let them practice one step at a time as they build toward their goal.
sources.supports: Break a new thing into small steps and practise one step at a time. The page is about worry in general; applied here to trying something new.

sources.title: My daughter is extremely shy and anxious around strangers. How can I help her?
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (Claire McCarthy, MD, FAAP, updated 9 Nov 2021)
sources.quote: Encourage your child to take small social "baby steps" like saying "hi" to a neighbor ... Give your child lots of praise and kudos for any accomplishment—even "baby steps" can be hard!
sources.supports: Small social baby steps such as saying hi, and praise for any accomplishment because even baby steps can be hard.

sources.title: Recommended Reading: Books to Teach Kids About Feelings & Resilience
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (updated 24 Apr 2025)
sources.quote: Reading books together about common feelings can help children recognize their own emotions.
sources.supports: Reading books together about feelings can help children recognise their own emotions; the page also says caregivers can apply a book's message to any new situation.

claims.supports: ZERO TO THREE: slow to warm up children are uneasy or cautious in new situations. The line is imagined inner voice, one possibility.

claims.wording_he: לספר מראש לאן הולכים ומי יהיה שם
claims.supports: ZERO TO THREE: give notice about new people, events and places; CHOP: tell the child about a new place before getting there.

claims.wording_he: לתרגל בבית איך נכנסים ואומרים שלום
claims.supports: Child Mind Institute: scripting, role-playing and previewing are excellent tools (page about social anxiety, applied as an analogy).
ZERO TO THREE: follow your child's lead and just watch the action for a while; Child Mind Institute: starting out watching the other kids.
ZERO TO THREE: put what you think your child is feeling into words.
KidsHealth: break a new thing into small steps and practise one step at a time; HealthyChildren.org: small social baby steps like saying hi.
HealthyChildren.org: give lots of praise for any accomplishment, even baby steps can be hard.

HealthyChildren.org: reading books together about feelings can help children recognise their own emotions, and a book's message can be applied to a new situation. That the story is personalised, with the child as the hero, is our wording.
The child's name is in the text and the child stars in every illustration (live site, 16 Oct 2026). No brand or title on the slide.

sources.title: Children with Shy or Slow to Warm Up Temperaments
sources.publisher: ZERO TO THREE (page dated 4 May 2025)
sources.quote: "slow to warm up," meaning they are uneasy or cautious in new situations or with unfamiliar people. ... Give notice about new people, events, and places. ... follow your child's lead and just watch the action for a while. ... gives a shy child some time to engage in side-by-side play ... Put what you think your child is feeling into words. ... Avoid labels. ... Routines are especially important and comforting.
sources.supports: Slow to warm up children are uneasy or cautious in new situations; tips: give notice about new people, events and places, follow the child's lead and let them watch, side-by-side play, name the feeling, avoid labels, keep routines. Quotes are fragments read through a page fetch, joined with ' ... '. The page is about shy or slow to warm up children in general (toddlers and preschoolers).

sources.title: Shyness in Kids
sources.publisher: CHOP (Children's Hospital of Philadelphia) health tip by Katie K. Lockwood, MD, MEd, 10 Jul 2025
sources.quote: For example, if you're headed to a new park or playground, tell your child about it before you get there ... When you get there, follow your child's lead. ... We have to be very careful about labeling kids or allowing others to label our kids as 'shy' or 'stand-offish'.
sources.supports: Tell the child about a new place before arriving, follow the child's lead when there, and be careful about labels such as shy. Fragments read through a page fetch.

sources.title: How to Help Young Children with Social Anxiety
sources.publisher: Child Mind Institute (Katherine Martinelli, reviewed 1 Jul 2026)
sources.quote: Scripting, role-playing and previewing are all excellent tools for the socially anxious kid. ... I'll encourage her to take little steps out of her comfort zone, like starting out watching the other kids,
sources.supports: Previewing and role-playing help a child who is nervous in social situations; a parent's example of little steps out of the comfort zone, starting by watching other kids. The page is about social anxiety; we apply the previewing and small steps to cautious children as an analogy, not as a diagnosis.

sources.title: Helping Kids When They Worry
sources.publisher: Nemours KidsHealth (reviewed Oct 2021 by Holly M. Antal, PhD)
sources.quote: When possible, help kids break a new thing into small steps. ... Let them practice one step at a time as they build toward their goal.
sources.supports: Break a new thing into small steps and practise one step at a time. The page is about worry in general; applied here to trying something new.

sources.title: My daughter is extremely shy and anxious around strangers. How can I help her?
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (Claire McCarthy, MD, FAAP, updated 9 Nov 2021)
sources.quote: Encourage your child to take small social "baby steps" like saying "hi" to a neighbor ... Give your child lots of praise and kudos for any accomplishment—even "baby steps" can be hard!
sources.supports: Small social baby steps such as saying hi, and praise for any accomplishment because even baby steps can be hard.

sources.title: Recommended Reading: Books to Teach Kids About Feelings & Resilience
sources.publisher: HealthyChildren.org, American Academy of Pediatrics (updated 24 Apr 2025)
sources.quote: Reading books together about common feelings can help children recognize their own emotions.
sources.supports: Reading books together about feelings can help children recognise their own emotions; the page also says caregivers can apply a book's message to any new situation.

claims.wording_he: במקום אל תפחדי משפט עם צעד
claims.supports: KidsHealth: break a new thing into small steps; ZERO TO THREE: name the feeling and follow the child's lead. That a sentence with a step is clearer than 'don't be afraid' is our reading, not a measured finding.

claims.wording_he: משפט עם צעד קטן נותן מקום להתחיל
claims.supports: KidsHealth: help kids break a new thing into small steps and practise one step at a time. Our wording.
ZERO TO THREE: follow your child's lead and just watch the action for a while; Child Mind Institute: starting out watching the other kids.
KidsHealth: let them practise one step at a time as they build toward their goal.
ZERO TO THREE and CHOP: tell the child beforehand; Child Mind Institute: role-playing and previewing.
ZERO TO THREE: put what you think your child is feeling into words.
ZERO TO THREE and CHOP: follow your child's lead.
HealthyChildren.org: lots of praise for any accomplishment, even baby steps can be hard.

HealthyChildren.org: reading books together about feelings can help children recognise their own emotions, and a book's message can be applied to a new situation. That the story is personalised, with the child as the hero, is our wording.
The child's name is in the text and the child stars in every illustration (live site, 16 Oct 2026). No brand or title on the slide.

hook.gap: How do you help a five year old try a new activity, and in what order?

character_anchor.child: A 5-year-old Israeli boy with short dark curly hair, olive skin, big brown eyes and a small gap between his front teeth.
character_anchor.parent: His mother, early thirties, tanned skin, dark wavy hair in a low bun, kind brown eyes, and his father, mid-thirties, short dark hair, light stubble and a calm smile; both warm and a little tired in a real way.
character_anchor.wardrobe: Boy: teal cotton T-shirt with a plain front and grey shorts, white sneakers. Mother: terracotta linen shirt and jeans. Father: light grey T-shirt and navy shorts.

image.beat: a wide, nervous grin at the door of a first class
image.action: The boy faces the viewer and looks straight into the camera with a giant, slightly nervous grin and raised eyebrows, holding a small blue water bottle with both hands; his parents are small and soft in the background beside a doorway.
image.setting: A bright hallway of an Israeli sports centre in the late afternoon: a plain pale wall, a bench with small bags, other children only as soft blurred shapes.
image.camera: Child eye level, close head-and-shoulders shot, the face large in the lower half of the frame.
image.lighting: Warm daylight through a window, muted gold.
image.wardrobe_objects: A small blue water bottle held by the boy in both hands.
